definition: The James–Lange theory is a historical psychology view that treats emotion as related to its bodily, outward expression, and is described as a peripheral or effect theory of emotion. It is named for William James and Carl Lange and became an important starting point for later discussion of emotion.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record James-Lange; pinned source text

reasons: The phrase “bodily, outward expression” goes beyond the packet, which only says the theory concerns emotion and its so-called expression; “bodily” is not supported.
The definition should stay strictly within the historical source wording and not add an extra characterization not found there.

The definition adds that the theory treats emotion as related to its “bodily, outward expression,” but the packet only states it is a “peripheral” or “effect theory” concerning the relation of emotion to its “so-called expression” and does not explicitly mention “bodily” or “outward.”
The definition’s phrase “peripheral or effect theory of emotion” is supported in substance, but the added bodily/outward wording is not directly supported by the packet.
